title: 1 Kings 18:30–46
context: Elijah repairs the LORD’s altar with twelve stones for the tribes of Jacob, drenches the offering with water three times, and at the time of the evening offering prays that the people may know the LORD is God and that he has turned their heart back again. The LORD’s fire falls and consumes everything, and the people fall on their faces confessing the LORD as God. Elijah then has the prophets of Baal seized and kills them at the brook Kishon, an act the narrative reports soberly and in line with the Mosaic penalty for prophets who led Israel to other gods (Deuteronomy 13:5). Elijah prays on Carmel, a small cloud rises from the sea, and a great rain falls as he runs before Ahab to Jezreel. In verse 37 the wording can be read as you are turning their heart back. Readers differ on how that turning relates to human response, as the notes at verse 37 explain, but Arminian and Reformed readers commonly read the whole as shared ground about the LORD answering prayer and calling his people back.

verses.text: Elijah said to all the people, “Come near to me!”; and all the people came near to him. He repaired the LORD’s altar that had been thrown down.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Elijah calling the people near and repairing the LORD’s altar that had been thrown down. Restoration begins with true worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the repaired altar as a sign of covenant renewal. Both traditions commonly read the verse as Elijah calling Israel back to the LORD.

verses.text: Elijah took twelve stones, according to the number of the tribes of the sons of Jacob, to whom the LORD’s word came, saying, “Israel shall be your name.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Elijah taking twelve stones for the tribes of Jacob, recalling the name Israel. Unity under God is restored symbolically.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the twelve stones as a reminder of God’s covenant with all Israel (compare Genesis 32:28). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as affirming the whole people’s identity.

verses.text: With the stones he built an altar in the LORD’s name. He made a trench around the altar large enough to contain two seahs of seed.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Elijah building the altar in the LORD’s name and digging a trench around it. Every detail is deliberate.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the altar as built according to God’s name and purpose. Both traditions commonly read the trench as preparing for the water that will make the miracle unmistakable.

verses.text: He put the wood in order, and cut the bull in pieces and laid it on the wood. He said, “Fill four jars with water, and pour it on the burnt offering and on the wood.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Elijah arranging the wood and bull and calling for water to be poured on the offering. He removes any doubt about the outcome.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the water as emphasizing that only God can bring fire. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as heightening the demonstration.

verses.text: He said, “Do it a second time;” and they did it the second time. He said, “Do it a third time;” and they did it the third time.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the water poured a second and third time. Elijah’s confidence in the LORD is evident to everyone watching.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the repetition as underlining God’s power beyond natural means. Both traditions commonly read the verse as building suspense.

verses.text: The water ran around the altar; and he also filled the trench with water.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the water running around the altar and filling the trench. The scene is set for a clear and unmistakable sign.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the soaked altar as making the coming fire undeniably the LORD’s work. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as completing Elijah’s preparation.

verses.text: At the time of the evening offering, Elijah the prophet came near and said, “LORD, the God of Abraham, of Isaac, and of Israel, let it be known today that you are God in Israel and that I am your servant, and that I have done all these things at your word.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Elijah praying at the evening offering that the LORD would show he is God and that Elijah is his servant. His prayer is simple and focused.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the prayer as seeking God’s glory above all. Both traditions commonly note the contrast between Elijah’s brief prayer and the long frenzy of Baal’s prophets.

verses.text: Hear me, LORD, hear me, that this people may know that you, LORD, are God, and that you have turned their heart back again.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Elijah asking that the people may know the LORD is God and that he has turned their heart back again. They commonly see God’s gracious call working on hearts that can respond.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the same words God’s own work in turning hearts (compare Deuteronomy 30:6; see also the Deuteronomy 10:16 discussion). Readers in both traditions commonly hold that any true turning of the heart is God’s gracious work, while differing on whether that grace can be resisted.

verses.text: Then the LORD’s fire fell and consumed the burnt offering, the wood, the stones, and the dust; and it licked up the water that was in the trench.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD’s fire falling and consuming the offering, wood, stones, dust, and water. God answers decisively.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the fire as an overwhelming display of the LORD’s sovereignty over creation. Both traditions commonly read the verse as the climax of the contest.

verses.text: When all the people saw it, they fell on their faces. They said, “The LORD, he is God! The LORD, he is God!”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the people falling on their faces and confessing that the LORD is God. The public confession answers the earlier silence.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the confession as the fruit of God’s revelation. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as the turning point for the people.

verses.text: Elijah said to them, “Seize the prophets of Baal! Don’t let one of them escape!” They seized them; and Elijah brought them down to the brook Kishon, and killed them there.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Elijah ordering the prophets of Baal seized and killing them at the brook Kishon. The text reports this plainly, in line with the Mosaic penalty for prophets who led Israel to other gods (Deuteronomy 13:5).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the act within Israel’s covenant law and its particular situation, not as a pattern for the church (compare Luke 9:54–55; 2 Corinthians 10:4). Both traditions commonly read the verse soberly, neither softening it nor celebrating violence.

verses.text: Elijah said to Ahab, “Get up, eat and drink; for there is the sound of abundance of rain.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Elijah telling Ahab to eat and drink because there is the sound of abundant rain. Promise precedes visible fulfillment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Elijah’s confidence as resting on God’s word in 18:1. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as faith anticipating God’s action.

verses.text: So Ahab went up to eat and to drink. Elijah went up to the top of Carmel; and he bowed himself down on the earth, and put his face between his knees.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Elijah going up Carmel and bowing with his face between his knees. He prays earnestly for rain (compare James 5:18).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see his prayer as the means God uses to bring what he has promised (see the Joshua 10:14 discussion). Both traditions commonly read the verse as a model of humble, persistent prayer.

verses.text: He said to his servant, “Go up now and look toward the sea.” He went up and looked, then said, “There is nothing.” He said, “Go again” seven times.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Elijah sending his servant seven times to look toward the sea. His persistence models prayer that keeps asking.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the repeated sending as faith waiting for God’s timing. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as encouragement to keep praying.

verses.text: On the seventh time, he said, “Behold, a small cloud, like a man’s hand, is rising out of the sea.” He said, “Go up, tell Ahab, ‘Get ready and go down, so that the rain doesn’t stop you.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see a small cloud like a man’s hand rising from the sea, and Elijah warning Ahab to go down before the rain. Small beginnings signal great answers.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the cloud as the first sign of God’s promised rain. Both traditions commonly read the verse as showing God’s faithfulness to his word.

verses.text: In a little while, the sky grew black with clouds and wind, and there was a great rain. Ahab rode, and went to Jezreel.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the sky growing black and a great rain falling as Ahab rides to Jezreel. The drought ends as God promised.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the rain as the LORD’s vindication over Baal, the supposed storm god. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as the fulfillment of 18:1.

verses.text: The LORD’s hand was on Elijah; and he tucked his cloak into his belt and ran before Ahab to the entrance of Jezreel.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD’s hand on Elijah as he runs before Ahab to Jezreel. God empowers his servant beyond natural strength.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD’s hand as divine enabling for an extraordinary task. Both traditions commonly read the verse as a striking close to the Carmel account.
